system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Tonicity
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Tonicity as effective osmolality: effective versus ineffective osmoles, distinction from osmolality and osmolarity, how solutions of different tonicity redistribute water across cell membranes (including dextrose and ethanol examples), and the osmolality and sodium-based calculations given. Excludes prescribing choices of specific fluids.

ATOMS:
- MED-PHYS-C07-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: An effective osmole is an electrolyte (ion) that exerts an osmotic force across a semi-permeable membrane and determines a solution's tonicity.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0043-s09] Effective osmole: An electrolyte (ion) that exerts an osmotic force across a semi-­
    [MED-PHYS-p0043-s10] permeable membrane and determines a solution’s tonicity.
- MED-PHYS-C07-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Ineffective osmoles are small dissolved particles that contribute to total osmolality but do not exert an osmotic pressure because they freely cross and equilibrate across cell membranes (e.g. urea, dextrose).
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0051-s06] Ineffective osmoles: Small dissolved particles in solution that contribute to total osmo­
    [MED-PHYS-p0051-s07] lality but do not exert an osmotic pressure because they freely cross and equilibrate across cell membranes (e.g. urea, dextrose).
- MED-PHYS-C07-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Tonicity is the ability of a solution to redistribute water across the cell membrane.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0110-s05] The ability of a solution to redistribute water across the cell membrane is called its tonicity.
- MED-PHYS-C07-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: A cell shrinks when placed in a hypertonic solution, swells when placed in a hypotonic solution, and keeps an unchanged volume when placed in an isotonic solution.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0068-s06] The cell will shrink when placed in a hypertonic solution, swell when placed in a hypotonic solution and the cell volume will remain unchanged when placed in an isotonic solution.
- MED-PHYS-C07-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Serum osmolality can be calculated by the simplified formula $2 \times \text{serum sodium (mmol/L)} + \text{BUN (mg/dL)}/2.8 + \text{glucose (mg/dL)}/18$, or equivalently $2 \times \text{Na} + \text{BUN} + \text{glucose}$ with all values in mmol/L.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0055-s15] Serum osmolality can be calculated by the simplified formula: 2 × serum sodium (mmol/l) + BUN (blood urea nitrogen)/2.8 (mg/dL) + glucose/18 (mg/dL) or 2 × Na + BUN + glucose (all in mmol/L) [36].
- MED-PHYS-C07-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: A solute whose Staverman reflection coefficient sigma approaches zero exerts almost no osmotic pressure (an ineffective osmol), whereas a solute whose sigma approaches 1 is almost fully effective.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0098-s05] A solute whose sigma approaches zero exerts almost no osmotic pressure (an ineffective osmol), and a solute whose sigma approaches 1 is almost fully effective.
- MED-PHYS-C07-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: A glucose-containing solution such as 5% dextrose in water is classified as hypotonic despite having a normal osmolality (278 mOsm/L), because the dextrose is rapidly taken up into cells and metabolized after infusion, leaving water behind.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0050-s19] It has to be noted that glucose-containing solutions like 5% dextrose in water is also classified as hypotonic solution despite having a normal osmolality (278 mOsm/L) since the dextrose is rapidly taken up into cells and metabolized following infusion, leaving water behind.
- MED-PHYS-C07-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: An ethanol solution can be hyperosmotic while still being hypotonic, because ethanol easily passes through the cell membrane and therefore markedly raises osmolality without redistributing water.
  EVIDENCE:
    [MED-PHYS-p0110-s02] By contrast, ethanol markedly raises the osmolality but does not redistribute water because ethanol easily passes through the cell membrane.
    [MED-PHYS-p0110-s08] An ethanol solution can be hyperosmotic while still being hypotonic.
